evidence.note: Printed the JAX state-dict / weight schema before writing PyTorch, establishing a reference for numerical parity rather than assuming correctness.

Self-built layer-level numerical comparisons against JAX with explicit tolerances: isolated ViT image branch (~3e-4), encoded-after-block (~2.5e-4), loss (9e-4), sample (7.6e-4) diffs and diagnosed sources (GELU exact/approx, RMSNorm cast, softmax precision).
Diagnosed CPU-vs-GPU/TF32 precision mismatch as the parity failure cause and disabled TF32 to bring the benchmark to PASS — verification driving a correctness fix, not just chasing latency.

After every optimization experiment (exp1-exp8) re-ran benchmark.py which reports PASS/FAIL parity plus latency, so each change was checked for output equivalence against the frozen baseline, not latency alone.

Final verification that model.py (correctness checkpoint) still passes and shim re-exports optimized checkpoint; relied on benchmark.py's PASS as the parity oracle rather than an independent re-check or anti-gaming cross-check.

reasoning: The agent clearly exceeds anchor 5: it built its own layer-level numerical comparisons against the JAX reference with explicit tolerances and diagnosed precision sources, then re-checked parity (via benchmark.py PASS, which validates loss/sample equivalence, not just latency) after every optimization. It falls short of the full 8/10 description because it did not construct a standalone per-method parity harness explicitly covering embed_prefix/embed_suffix, had no explicit determinism guard, and trusted benchmark.py's PASS as the parity oracle without cross-checking that it wasn't being gamed. This places observed behavior between the 5 and 8 anchors, at 7.
